title: Valid Parentheses
understanding: You get a string of brackets: round, square, and curly. Decide whether every opening bracket is closed by the correct type, in the correct order, with nothing left over.

hint_ladder.l1: When you meet a closing bracket, which opening bracket must it match? Is it always the most recent unmatched opener, or could it be an older one?
hint_ladder.l2: The rule 'a closer must match the most recently opened, still-unmatched bracket' should feel like a specific ordering discipline. What everyday structure enforces last-in, first-out?
hint_ladder.l3: Keep track of the openers you've seen but not yet closed. On a closer, only the one at the top of that pile is allowed to match. What has to be true of the pile when the string ends?
hint_ladder.l4: Push each opener onto a pile. On each closer, check the top of the pile is its partner and remove it; if it isn't, or the pile is empty, it's invalid. At the very end the pile must be empty.

approaches.name: Stack
approaches.idea: Push openers; on a closer, pop and verify the popped opener matches. Valid iff the stack is empty at the end.

pitfalls.mistake: Using only counts of open vs close
pitfalls.symptom: Passes simple cases, fails interleaved brackets

pitfalls.mistake: Forgetting the empty-stack check on a closer
pitfalls.why: A leading closer has nothing to match
pitfalls.symptom: Index/pop error or wrong True on ']'

pitfalls.mistake: Not requiring the stack to be empty at the end

failure_cases.mistake: Counting brackets instead of matching them
failure_cases.why: The counts balance perfectly — one of each, opened before closed. Counting is blind to nesting order, which is the entire problem.

failure_cases.mistake: Popping without checking the stack is empty
failure_cases.why: A closer arrives with nothing open. You have to treat an empty stack as an immediate 'invalid', not reach into it.
No closer ever mismatched, because no closer ever arrived. Two openers are still unmatched when the string ends.

failure_cases.mistake: Matching against any open bracket rather than the most recent
failure_cases.why: Only the top of the stack is a legal partner. Scanning for any unmatched opener throws away the LIFO discipline the problem is built on.

edge_cases: Correct types but wrong order, like '([)]'
rewrite_challenges: Support a fourth bracket type by changing only the pairs map — verify nothing else needs to move.
Return the index of the first offending bracket instead of a boolean.
Solve it without an explicit stack for a single bracket type — why doesn't that generalize to three types?
